summary: A discussion of the print file type in the ARPANET File Transfer Protocol, written before an FTP meeting. It reviews how vertical format control for printed output should be treated, and how the Remote Job Entry protocol seemed to force one particular interpretation. It updates RFC 354, 385 and 454.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 448 explains why FTP's “print file” type was unclear. It distinguishes files with no printer controls, ASCII formatting controls, or ASA controls, then presents two possible ways to represent them in FTP.

questions: ftp type a e i l
subtitle: A discussion of how FTP should represent files with printer format controls.

tldr.problem: FTP's two file-format cases did not clearly represent the three ways printer processes handle vertical format control information.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes cases N, T, and A and shows how the Remote Job Entry protocol maps each case to FTP format and structure attributes.
tldr.outcome: It presents two choices: change the default file structure to record structure or add three FTP formats corresponding to the three printer cases.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 448's status as Unknown and no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. The RFC presents two possible changes and does not state which one was adopted.

sections.title: What Makes a File a Print File
sections.content:
A print file is intended for a printer and contains information that controls the vertical layout of a page, such as line spacing, overprinting, and page ejection. RFC 448 reviews a disagreement about how FTP should represent such files and says the RJE protocol seemed to force an interpretation that many FTP implementers might not expect.

The memo identifies three cases. Case N contains no vertical format control and lets the printer apply a standard format. Case T uses ASCII carriage return, line feed, and form feed controls. Case A places an ASA vertical-format-control code at the start of each record.
sections.plainLanguage: A print file may contain instructions for spacing, overprinting, or starting a new page. The memo distinguishes three ways those instructions can be represented.

sections.title: Why FTP's Two Cases Were Not Enough
sections.content:
RFC 454 appears to provide two FTP cases: unformatted and print file. RFC 448 says it is unclear how these correspond to the three RJE cases or whether the format describes the file as transferred or as stored by the server.

The distinction matters across systems. The memo says Tenex supports Case T, while IBM operating systems support Cases N and A and need to know whether a stored file has the internal print-file attribute. The server must decide whether to mark a received file accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: FTP offered two categories, but printers used three different ways to handle formatting. Servers therefore did not have a clear way to map every incoming file to the right stored form.

sections.title: RJE's Mapping and Two Possible Fixes
sections.content:
The RJE protocol maps Case N to unformatted format with record structure, Case T to unformatted format with file structure, and Case A to print-file format with record structure. This uses the structure attribute to distinguish Cases N and T.

For consistency, a server using ASA controls internally could convert every unformatted, unstructured file into an internal print file, which would imply changing FTP's default structure to record structure. The alternative is to add three FTP formats corresponding to Cases N, A, and T, and change RJE to match. RFC 448 presents these as choices for discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: RJE uses FTP's structure setting to distinguish files with no controls from files with ASCII controls. The memo suggests either changing FTP's default or adding a separate format for each of the three cases.
